title: Watson & Crick: The Spiral Staircase of Life
source_book: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid (Nature, Vol. 171)
source_author: J. D. Watson & F. H. C. Crick
authenticity_note: Based on James Watson and Francis Crick's historic April 25, 1953 Nature paper proposing the double-helical model of DNA with complementary base pairs (Adenine-Thymine, Guanine-Cytosine).
summary: On February 28, 1953, inside the Cavendish Laboratory at Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick fit cardboard cutouts of nucleotides together like puzzle pieces. Discovering that Adenine bonds only with Thymine, and Guanine with Cytosine, they burst into The Eagle pub announcing: 'We have found the secret of life!'
content:
In late 1952, at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, England, 24-year-old American ornithologist-turned-geneticist James Watson and 36-year-old British physicist Francis Crick were racing against the world's most famous chemist, Linus Pauling, to solve the structure of DNA.

Pauling had mistakenly published a model proposing a triple helix with the phosphate groups in the center. Watson and Crick knew that chemically, negatively charged phosphates crammed together in the core would violently repel each other. The spine had to be on the outside!

Armed with Rosalind Franklin's critical X-ray diffraction measurements—which gave the helix a width of 2.0 nanometers and a repeat period of 3.4 nanometers—Watson sat at a desk cutting out scale shapes of the four nitrogenous bases from cardboard: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), and Cytosine (C).

On the morning of February 28, 1953, Watson shifted the cardboard pieces across the table. Suddenly, he noticed that an Adenine-Thymine pair held together by two hydrogen bonds formed the *exact same physical width and geometric shape* as a Guanine-Cytosine pair held by hydrogen bonds!

Crick leaped from his chair. If A always paired with T, and G always paired with C, then the two strands were complementary mirror images of one another! If one strand had the sequence AGTC, the other strand automatically read TCAG.

At lunchtime, Crick burst through the door of The Eagle pub on Benet Street and famously proclaimed to the stunned patrons: *"We have found the secret of life!"*

On April 25, 1953, their one-page paper appeared in *Nature*. It contained the most famous understatement in the history of science:
*"It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material."*

When a cell divides, the double helix unzips down the middle, and each strand acts as a template to rebuild its perfect twin. In one stroke, Watson and Crick explained how living things reproduce, evolve, and pass life down through billions of years.

stem_vocabulary.definition: Chargaff's rules stating that DNA bases always pair specifically: Adenine with Thymine ($A-T$) and Guanine with Cytosine ($G-C$).
Weak chemical bonds forming between the complementary base pairs holding the two strands of DNA together.
The orientation of the two strands of DNA running in opposite directions ($5' \to 3'$ and $3' \to 5'$).
The sequence of nucleotide bases in DNA that dictates the amino acid sequence of proteins.
